title: Zoom in on CX Podcast: The "Purposeful Friction" Trick That Builds Customer Trust
summary: AI is changing every customer conversation—but is it building trust or breaking it? Ben Neo sits down with Leigh Hopwood, CEO of the CCMA, to unpack why trust is becoming the defining differentiator in customer experience.
body_markdown:
Customer experience leaders have heard the promises before: a new technology arrives, gets hyped as transformative, and ends up eroding the very trust it was supposed to build. First it was the IVR. Then chatbots. Now, as AI reshapes contact centres at speed, the question isn't whether AI belongs in customer experience — it's whether it will repeat history or finally get it right. Leigh Hopwood, CEO of the CCMA (Call Centre Management Association), joined Zoom in on CX to unpack why trust, not technology, is the real differentiator in modern CX strategy.


## Why AI Could Be the Industry's "Third Car Crash"


Hopwood doesn't mince words about the contact centre's track record with new technology. "I have been known to talk about AI being our third car crash," she explains. The first, she says, was the IVR — introduced as groundbreaking, but now synonymous with the dreaded "press one for this, press two for that." The second was chatbots, deployed to reduce cost but often failing to deliver a quality conversation.


The risk with AI in customer service, according to Hopwood, is repeating the same mistake: rolling out the technology without ensuring it actually serves the customer. But she's optimistic this time is different — AI, she argues, could be the catalyst that brings trust back onto the boardroom agenda, precisely because the stakes and visibility are so much higher.

## The Research: Customer Service Is Actually Getting Better


One of the more surprising findings Hopwood shared comes from CCMA's own research, conducted with support from Zoom. Contrary to the common narrative of declining service standards, the data — tracked over five years — shows contact centre customer service is genuinely improving, and consumer acceptance of self-service is strengthening alongside it.


"There's a real opportunity for us to lean into that," Hopwood says, "and make sure that we continue to build the trust that we are starting to see when people get in touch with contact centres." For CX leaders, this reframes the conversation: the goal isn't just damage control, it's building on genuine momentum.


## Why "Purposeful Friction" Builds Trust


Perhaps the most counterintuitive insight from the conversation: removing all friction from the customer journey isn't always the right goal. Hopwood makes the case for what she calls "purposeful friction" — deliberate checkpoints that reassure customers a brand is being careful with their money or data.


She points to banking as the clearest example. A frictionless process to move a large sum of money might sound efficient, but it can actually undermine trust. "If you could easily move five grand from one place to another without any questions, you might wonder — has that actually happened?" Hopwood says. Compare that to retail, where low margins and low-stakes transactions mean speed matters more than scrutiny. The lesson for CX strategy: friction should be calibrated to risk and emotional weight, not eliminated universally.


## Keeping Humans in the Loop


Even as AI in customer service matures, Hopwood is firm that human interaction isn't a nostalgic holdover — it's a necessity. "We need to keep the human in the loop," she says, "not out of nostalgia... we need them out of necessity." She describes four distinct buckets where AI can add value in CX: customer-facing support (the highest risk, highest reward), augmenting human agents with better information, back-office process automation, and surfacing insights from customer behaviour across the whole business — not just contact centre interactions.


## Key Takeaways


Customer service quality is measurably improving, according to five years of CCMA research:


- AI adoption in CX carries real risk of repeating past mistakes (IVR, chatbots) if implemented without care
- "Purposeful friction" — not frictionless design — is often what builds customer trust
- Friction should scale with the emotional or financial stakes of the interaction
- Human agents remain essential for authentic, complex, or sensitive conversations
- The biggest opportunity for CX leaders is using cross-business insights to build trust, not just optimising the contact centre in isolation
